Spike awoke to Buffy moaning and flailing on the bed—and not in the good way.

He sprung to his feet, on guard for whatever had infiltrated their lair, but saw nothing. Invisible demons? Ghosts?

“Ow ow ow oooooooow!” Buffy grunted through clenched teeth. She was half-twisted on her side, with her left leg bent up behind her tight. She was trying to push it flat, her face scrunched up in pain. Spike got on his knees beside her on the bed, trying to help push.

A screech escaped Buffy’s lips. Panicky, Spike tried a different tack, digging his fingers deep into Buffy’s calf, trying to unlock the seizing muscle. For a few moments Buffy kept screeching, but then her leg started at last to lower, and the screeches turned to whimpers. Her whole body relaxed, and she slumped back on her stomach. Spike continued to work her calf with one hand, while the other gently pushed it back on the bed.

The whimper became a little moan of relief.

And oh.

He was in bed. With Buffy. He was in bed with Buffy, and he was touching her. Touching her leg. Massaging her leg. He actually hadn’t been hard when he awoke, but he was achieving the state rapidly. He looked warily over at Buffy, but her face was soft, the removal of the pain making her woozy.

He kept massaging her calf, gentling his fingers a bit, wondering what this would feel like without the thick tights. In a second it was all laid out in his mind—work the massage up to her thighs, then up under her skirt where it was twisted around her, stroke that dark, warm place that occupied his fantasies, how she’d moan and whimper with pleasure then, how she’d want him, how she’d turn to embrace him—

He had shifted on his knees, angled over her. Skipping a few steps, there, mate. Slow. Careful. Work up to it. Do it right. He was tingling, from his groin out to the tips of his fingers, still rubbing slow circles into her muscles. This was happening. This was happening.

Centimeter by centimeter, he inched towards the back of her knees. She was breathing heavily, still recovering. Spike shifted again, trying to ease the pressure on his prick, give himself room to think, to stick with the plan. Good plan.

Except that the creak of the mattress roused her. “Um, Spike?”

He froze, eyes glued to the back of her thigh. So close.

“I’m good now.”

“Yeah.” He sounded weirdly breathy.

It’s not that Buffy didn’t appreciate his help—she hadn’t had one in years, but Charlie horses hurt like a bitch—but it was unsettling when he hovered over her, like a man on a diet slavering over a hamburger. She was really trying to play nice with Spike. Being reminded she was his favorite meal wasn’t helping.

Although, damn, could the man give a massage. She’d missed that luxury, since Riley had left. Even if the last few months’ worth hadn’t been quite as effective, just the act of being touched, soothed, worried over had been healing. Spike touching her like that… it bothered her.

“Get off the bed, Spike,” she said quietly, with just enough steel to get her point across.

Spike gripped her calf, just a little too hard, enough to remind her of his strength, not enough to set off the chip. Domineering jerk. He made some kind of noise and then the mattress creaked and he was off at last. Buffy laid still, trying to let the grief ebb back out of her, gently flexing and pointing her ankle to keep her calf muscle relaxed. She decided to focus on that.

“Sorry about the wake-up call,” she said at last, sounding more concerned for her pride than his beauty sleep. “Muscle cramps are the worst. You know I got thrown two stories up a wall awhile back and it didn’t hurt half so much?”

Concern crushed the vestiges of Spike’s thwarted arousal. “You what now?”

“The demon I asked you to watch out for.”

“You didn’t tell me she was that bad.”

“Well, she is.” Buffy trailed off, her face drawn with worry. “So I have to get back. To protect… to protect everyone.”

Spike turned away to hide his smile. He loved the way she got all protective, tiny and fierce and violent. He could still remember the way she had looked when he was hurt when she’d loved him—when she’d been spelled into loving him, remember that bit, Spike—and to have her look at him that way again… God, what he wouldn’t give.

“—but the thing I don’t understand is why my feet hurt so bad. I haven’t done anything here. Could it be a side effect of the time travel? Like jetlag for feet? Feetlag?”

Spike cocked his head. Perhaps he could offer a footrub? Get them back on track with the massages? Feet could be very erotic. Concerned for their friend’s well-being, the two girls rang the doorbell repeatedly, but there was no response. Yuri hesitantly reached for the doorknob, finding it surprisingly unlocked. They exchanged worried glances before cautiously entering Natsuki’s house.

Inside, the house was strangely silent. The air felt heavy with tension as they made their way through the dimly lit hallway. They called out Natsuki’s name, but there was still no answer.

As they moved closer to Natsuki’s room, they noticed a faint flickering light under the door. Yuri and Monika exchanged another glance, their worry increasing with every step.

Finally, with trembling hands, Yuri pushed open the door. What they saw inside left them frozen in shock. Natsuki sat on the floor, surrounded by piles of empty spider carcasses - and she was eating one of them. Her usually cheerful face was now gaunt and pale, her eyes vacant.

Yuri and Monika stood in the doorway, their hearts pounding in their chests. The room seemed to close in around them as they took in the horrifying sight before them. They had known Natsuki as a tough, no-nonsense girl with a love for manga, but this was something they never could have anticipated.

“Natsuki…” Monika managed to choke out, her voice barely above a whisper. “What…what happened to you?”

Natsuki’s head slowly turned towards them, her mouth still full of spider. She blinked, as if struggling to recognize her friends. A hollow, detached voice echoed from her lips.

“Hungry…” she mumbled, her words barely audible. “Must…feed…”

Yuri and Monika exchanged worried glances, realizing that something had clearly gone terribly wrong with their friend. They cautiously approached Natsuki, trying to hide their fear as they attempted to understand the situation.

“Natsuki, please, snap out of it,” Yuri pleaded softly, her voice trembling. “You don’t have to do this. We can help you.”

But Natsuki seemed oblivious to their words, her focus solely on the spiders crawling around her. She picked up another lifeless carcass and brought it closer to her mouth, her actions mechanical and devoid of any emotion.

Monika took a step forward, her voice laced with desperation. “Natsuki, listen to me. We care about you, and we want to help. Something is clearly wrong, and we need to get you out of here.”

Natsuki’s vacant eyes briefly met Monika’s gaze before flickering away. Her grip on the dead spider tightened, and she began to chew it, swallowing with an unnerving lack of disgust.

Feeling a mix of fear and determination, Yuri took a deep breath and stepped further into the room. “Natsuki, we need to bring you back to the club. We can figure this out together. Please, let us help you.”

Natsuki’s gaze shifted towards Yuri, her eyes now reflecting a flicker of recognition. A momentary spark of humanity seemed to ignite within her, her vacant expression momentarily replaced with a glimmer of sadness.

“Hungry… always hungry,” Natsuki whispered, her voice still detached and hollow. “Must…eat…spiders…to sustain self…”

Yuri and Monika exchanged worried glances, their hearts breaking at the sight of their friend’s suffering. They both knew they had to act quickly to help Natsuki, to bring her back from whatever dark abyss she had fallen into.

Gently, Yuri reached out her hand towards Natsuki, her voice filled with empathy. “Natsuki, I understand that you feel like you need to do this to survive, but there must be another way. We can find a better solution together. Please, let us help you.”

Natsuki’s vacant eyes met Yuri’s for a brief moment, her grip on the dead spider loosening ever so slightly. A flicker of hope sparked within Yuri’s heart as she saw a small glimmer of the old Natsuki breaking through the darkness.

Monika, sensing the opportunity, joined Yuri’s side, her voice filled with determination. “We care about you, Natsuki. We don’t want to see you suffer like this. Let us be there for you, just like you were there for us. We can find a way to save you.”

Natsuki blinked, a tear escaping her empty eyes as a glimpse of her former self fought to resurface. “I…I can’t stop,” she whispered, her voice filled with anguish. “I can’t control…the hunger!”

Natsuki immediately lunged at Monika - killing her instantly.

It’s been 4 days since that unfortunate day. Unwilling to come to terms with the death of his childhood friend, MC threw himself off a building.

But one day, one of the club members - Natsuki - noticed something while passing by Sayori’s house. It looked like…the corpse of a spider.

As they moved closer to Natsuki’s room, they noticed a faint flickering light under the door. Yuri and Monika exchanged another glance, their worry increasing with every step.

Finally, with trembling hands, Yuri pushed open the door. What they saw inside left them frozen in shock. Natsuki sat on the floor, surrounded by piles of empty spider carcasses - and she was eating one of them. Her usually cheerful face was now gaunt and pale, her eyes vacant.

Yuri and Monika stood in the doorway, their hearts pounding in their chests. The room seemed to close in around them as they took in the horrifying sight before them. They had known Natsuki as a tough, no-nonsense girl with a love for manga, but this was something they never could have anticipated.

“Natsuki…” Monika managed to choke out, her voice barely above a whisper. “What…what happened to you?”

Natsuki’s head slowly turned towards them, her mouth still full of spider. She blinked, as if struggling to recognize her friends. A hollow, detached voice echoed from her lips.

“Hungry…” she mumbled, her words barely audible. “Must…feed…”

Yuri and Monika exchanged worried glances, realizing that something had clearly gone terribly wrong with their friend. They cautiously approached Natsuki, trying to hide their fear as they attempted to understand the situation.

“Natsuki, please, snap out of it,” Yuri pleaded softly, her voice trembling. “You don’t have to do this. We can help you.”

But Natsuki seemed oblivious to their words, her focus solely on the spiders crawling around her. She picked up another lifeless carcass and brought it closer to her mouth, her actions mechanical and devoid of any emotion.

Monika took a step forward, her voice laced with desperation. “Natsuki, listen to me. We care about you, and we want to help. Something is clearly wrong, and we need to get you out of here.”

Natsuki’s vacant eyes briefly met Monika’s gaze before flickering away. Her grip on the dead spider tightened, and she began to chew it, swallowing with an unnerving lack of disgust.

Feeling a mix of fear and determination, Yuri took a deep breath and stepped further into the room. “Natsuki, we need to bring you back to the club. We can figure this out together. Please, let us help you.”

Natsuki’s gaze shifted towards Yuri, her eyes now reflecting a flicker of recognition. A momentary spark of humanity seemed to ignite within her, her vacant expression momentarily replaced with a glimmer of sadness.

“Hungry… always hungry,” Natsuki whispered, her voice still detached and hollow. “Must…eat…spiders…to sustain self…”

Yuri and Monika exchanged worried glances, their hearts breaking at the sight of their friend’s suffering. They both knew they had to act quickly to help Natsuki, to bring her back from whatever dark abyss she had fallen into.

Gently, Yuri reached out her hand towards Natsuki, her voice filled with empathy. “Natsuki, I understand that you feel like you need to do this to survive, but there must be another way. We can find a better solution together. Please, let us help you.”

Natsuki’s vacant eyes met Yuri’s for a brief moment, her grip on the dead spider loosening ever so slightly. A flicker of hope sparked within Yuri’s heart as she saw a small glimmer of the old Natsuki breaking through the darkness.

Monika, sensing the opportunity, joined Yuri’s side, her voice filled with determination. “We care about you, Natsuki. We don’t want to see you suffer like this. Let us be there for you, just like you were there for us. We can find a way to save you.”

Natsuki blinked, a tear escaping her empty eyes as a glimpse of her former self fought to resurface. “I…I can’t stop,” she whispered, her voice filled with anguish. “I can’t control…the hunger!”

Natsuki immediately lunged at Monika - killing her instantly.

As she held the amulet, Yuri’s mind filled with visions of Natsuki, tormented and trapped by her insatiable hunger. She made a silent promise to her friend that she would do whatever it took to set her free.

Using the knowledge she had gained through her research, Yuri began to unravel the ancient incantations hidden within the amulet. With each word she spoke, she could feel the amulet’s power intensify, granting her the ability to bend reality to her will.

With newfound confidence, Yuri returned to her town, ready to face the challenges that lay ahead. She knew that Spider Eater Natsuki would not be easily defeated, but she had the strength of the amulet on her side.

Gathering the remaining members of the Literature Club, Yuri shared her plan to save Natsuki. She explained the legend behind the Arachnid Amulet and their role in helping bring their friend back from the darkness.

Together, the club members worked tirelessly to create a trap, using their combined knowledge and talents. They scoured the town for a special ingredient that Yuri believed could help neutralize the cursed hunger within Natsuki.

On a moonlit night, they lured Spider Eater Natsuki to a secluded location, where they had set up the trap. With bated breath, they watched as Natsuki’s vacant eyes scanned the area, her hunger seemingly insatiable.

Taking a deep breath, Yuri stepped forward, holding out the special ingredient they had found. It was a rare herb that had the power to nullify the cursed hunger.

“Natsuki,” Yuri called out, her voice filled with determination. “We want to help you. We know you’re still in there, fighting. Please, take this. It will end your suffering.”

Natsuki’s eyes flickered with recognition, a glimmer of humanity hidden beneath the darkness. However, the curse had taken over her - and she started to attack Yuri.

Yuri dodged Natsuki’s attacks, narrowly avoiding the sharp claws that extended from her fingertips. With agility granted by the Arachnid Amulet, Yuri danced around Natsuki, her movements swift and precise.

Using her heightened strength, Yuri grabbed Natsuki’s arm and held it firmly, her eyes locked with her friend’s vacant gaze. “Natsuki, I know you’re still in there,” Yuri pleaded, her voice filled with determination. “Fight the hunger. You can overcome this.”

Natsuki’s struggling momentarily ceased, a flicker of recognition crossing her eyes. As Yuri held her gaze, she slowly extended her other hand, offering the herb once more. “Natsuki, please,” Yuri urged. “Take this. It can help you regain control.”

In a moment of clarity, Natsuki took the herb from Yuri’s outstretched hand. But instead of eating it, Natsuki threw it into a nearby pool of lava. She shifted her gaze towards Yuri. “GIVE ME...” Natsuki menacingly said "...MY AMULET!"

         limited_tasks.task,
         limited_tasks.answer,
         array_agg(DISTINCT classes.name) AS class_name,
         array_agg(DISTINCT topics.name) AS topic_name,
         array_agg(DISTINCT authors.name) AS authors_name

    (SELECT *,
         unnest(path) AS linked_id

INNER JOIN classes
    ON classes.id = tasks_classes.classes_id
INNER JOIN tasks_authors
    ON limited_tasks.id = tasks_authors.tasks_id

    ON authors.id = tasks_authors.authors_id
GROUP BY  limited_tasks.id, limited_tasks.task, limited_tasks.answer

user_prompt:
1.	Introduction
Verbal near synonym has been the hot issue in Mandarin lexical semantics. Most of previous studies focuses on the progress of the event structure, such as Module-Attribute Representation of Verbal Semantics (MARVS) proposed by Huang et al. (1994). Few studies, however, focus on the lexical meaning and domain with the comparison among verbal near synonyms. 
According to Chang (2013), the suggestion for the further studies recommends qíwàng and pànwàng as lexical targets to compare the lexical difference because of the closer but different lexical meaning. Therefore, this paper investigates the temporal property of pànwàng with the comparison of two verbal near synonyms, qíwàng and pànwàng in Mandarin Chinese. 
With the account of Li & Lin (2021), the corpora investigation is adopted in this paper. The temporal realization that pànwàng brings is presented by the temporal adverbs collocated with pànwàng in the corpus data. 翻译以下内容为中文：GENERAL REQUIREMENTS

There are two types of work activities:

•	DEAD WORK - Work with an electrical installation where there is no risk of being exposed to an electrical hazard and where work can be undertaken safely without requiring the entire specialist electrical working procedures. Regardless, risk assessment must be performed as part of these operations and isolation will be required. 

•	LIVE WORK - Work with an electrical installation where there is a risk of being exposed to an electrical hazard (for example, replacement of electrical equipment) and where appropriate working procedures need to be applied with full consideration of Section 5.4 .  

7.1	Dead Working 

All work on electric installations in vehicles MUST be carried out dead, except for the special circumstances detailed in Section 5.4.  Persons carrying out electrical work must be competent to do so and authorised or under the supervision of an authorised person. 

Each electrical installation in a vehicle must have a defined and documented Safe Isolation process which should be followed by an authorised person. Only those who also hold Electrical Safety without Hazardous Voltage (Orange badge) or IMI Level 3 Award  in Electrically Propelled Vehicle Repair and Replacement or higher are authorised to perform such operations in vehicles. The following standard process may be applied but it is important to note that there are differences to and from each vehicle and it must be confirmed before completing the isolation. 

•	Power-off the electrical installation by removal of the control signal - The control signal to the electrical installation must be turned off (key-off or similar) and the ELV power supply must be removed prior to continuing with the remaining activities.

•	Disconnect all external power sources - The electrical installation at which the work activity is to be carried out shall be disconnected from all external power sources (off-board charger, grid connections, etc.). The disconnection shall consist of an air gap or similar insulation which ensures that the point of disconnection cannot be bridged electrically. The point of disconnection shall be visually verifiable.

•	Verify absence of operating voltage - The absence of operating voltage shall be verified on all poles of the electrical installation. Built-in or portable equipment can, for example, be used for the dead verification check. Portable equipment shall be inspected immediately prior to and, if possible, after use. The equipment shall be suitable for the purpose.

•	Disconnect all internal power sources - The electrical installation at which the work shall be carried out shall be disconnected from all internal power sources (ESS” Energy Storage System”, electric machine driven by vehicle’s combustion engine, etc.). The disconnection shall consist of an air gap or similar insulation which ensures that the point of disconnection cannot be bridged electrically. The point of disconnection shall be visually verifiable.

•	Secure against re-connection (blocking) - All means that have been used to disconnect the electrical installation part for the work shall be blocked and locked. If there is no locking device, an equivalent blocking action shall be taken. A sign prohibiting unauthorized operation shall be put up. The sign shall state who has locked the electrical installation and explain that work is in progress. A record of the secured isolation must be clearly documented on the facility isolation and lock out register

























                                          HV Cable Lockout Device with Signage


•	Permission to Start work after decommissioning - Permission from the nominated person in control of work activity and, if needed, from the nominated person in control of electric vehicle safety is required before work after decommissioning can start.

Commissioning after Work - After the work activity has been completed and inspected, personnel involved in the work activity shall be notified that the work activity has been completed and no more work is permitted. All tools, equipment and devices used during the work shall be removed. Only then shall the procedure for commissioning be commenced and the electrical installation shall be regarded as live. All safety equipment and/or devices at the work location shall be removed. Starting from the work location and progressing outwards, the equipment and/or devices that were applied to the electrical installation shall be removed and all the locks or other devices, which were used to prevent reconnection shall also be removed. All signs used for the work activity shall be removed. Only the person who has applied the isolation and lockout is authorised to remove it. A tag should be used along with the lock to record who applied the isolation. In the event that that person is unavailable Absent Person Lockout Removal Form must be completed in its entirety including the relevant authorisations to remove the lock. 

7.2	Live Working

Any work conducted on or in the vicinity of live electrical installations in vehicles that are accessible requires a completed Live Electrical Work Permit. This includes all diagnostic testing when no alternative testing method is available. The permit must be completed in its entirety including the risk assessment exercise. 

Only those with Electrical Safety with Hazardous Voltage (Blue Badge) or IMI Level 4 Award in the Diagnosis, Testing and Repair of Electric Vehicles and Components are permitted to perform work on live HV EV systems and equipment subject to the approval of the relevant live working permit. Those who are authorised to issue permits are defined in Responsible Persons Register. Under no circumstances can the person who issued the live working permit also be the person in Control of the work activity. 

The exemption to the requirements for a permit to work is in the case of manufacturing where consistent repeatable operations are performed where hazards are understood, and risk assessed. This does not remove the requirements for contact protection. Any abnormal condition within the manufacturing environment must be considered. 

7.2.1	Is it unreasonable for the work to be done dead?

There are some circumstances where it is unreasonable to make equipment dead because of the difficulties it would cause. For example, it may be difficult, if not impossible, to commission a complex control system without having it energised at some time with parts live (but not exposed so that they may be easily touched). Also, it may not be realistic to monitor the operation and performance of a control system or to trace a malfunction of such equipment with it dead, i.e., fault-finding.

7.2.2	Identify and Assess the Risks and Methods for Controlling them

At this stage some form of formal risk assessment is necessary. This will 	usually be qualitative, but it should be applied to the specific equipment to be worked on or nearby. The person carrying out the assessment etc. should have extensive knowledge and experience of the factors to consider and of the competence of the people who will be carrying out the work and of their ability to avoid danger. 

7.2.3	Decide if it Reasonable to Work Live

On completion of the preceding stage, it is now appropriate for managers and supervisors to judge whether it is reasonable in all circumstances to work live. The decision should not be taken lightly. At this stage the economic and operational factors should be evaluated against the risks involved before deciding, bearing in mind that the shock or burn risks associated with working live can be very serious. This decision will result in a permit to work being issued or declined. 

7.2.4	Decide whether suitable precautions can be taken to prevent injury

Providing these requirements have been met, live working can still only be justified if suitable precautions are taken to prevent injury arising from risks identified in the assessment. These MUST be specified in the permit to work. 

The possibility of anyone touching parts at dangerously different potentials at the same time should be avoided by installing temporary insulation or protective barriers. This may mean putting temporary insulating screens over live parts and/or applying insulation to parts that are at earth potential. Temporary screens etc. can also help to prevent the risk of accidental short circuit from tools, components, conductors etc.

When work is to be carried out ‘near’ rather than ‘on’ live equipment the essential precautions will often be directed towards ensuring that appropriate and adequate safety clearances are established and maintained. 

The people doing the work must be adequately trained and experienced in the type of live work being undertaken. They should understand the task and be able to recognise any deterioration in the state of equipment or departures from agreed procedures. They should have the self-discipline to recognise their own limitations and should be encouraged to seek assistance with work that may be outside their area of competence.

There must be adequate working space and adequate lighting. There should be adequate headroom, no tripping hazards and no obstructions that could restrict a person’s movements. 

Only properly insulated tools should be used. They should have insulation that is robust enough to be proof against mechanical damage. These tools will be inspected by the user for abnormality prior to use. They will be destroyed if the insulation is damaged. Test instruments should have insulated probes and fused leads.

Protective clothing and equipment should be provided and used where this would reduce the risk of contact with live parts or earth. 

Experience has shown that rapid action can save life in the event of electric shock. A person working on live parts must be accompanied by someone who is in a safe position, who has the necessary competence to avoid injury, who can help by disconnecting the supply and who can render first aid or obtain assistance in the event of an emergency.

7.3	Environmental Conditions

Restrictions shall be applied to live working in the event of adverse environmental conditions. These restrictions are based on the reduction of insulating properties and on reduced visibility and impaired movement of the person(s) performing the work. If the work must be conducted outdoors, restrictions shall be made in the event of adverse weather conditions e.g., thunderstorms, high humidity, or rain. 

7.4	Tooling and Personal Protective Equipment 

Tools, equipment, and protective devices including PPE are clearly defined in the Polestar Global Standard for Working with Hazardous Voltages. Tooling and PPE should be subject to periodic visual inspection to ensure its continued suitability for use. 

7.5	Safety Equipment

In each building where work is performed electrical installations on vehicles Live or dead, the following safety equipment must be present.

•	Electrically Insulated Rescue Hook
•	Defibrillator
•	Suitable Barriers to restrict access all around the vehicle to unauthorised persons
•	Signage to indicate status of Electrical Installation of Vehicle

7.6	First Aid Provision

As a minimum there must be at least one First Aid at Work Trained persons at all times when work is being conducted under a live electrical permit. That person must have knowledge of the location of the rescue hook and the defibrillator. 

7.7	Signage

Not all hazards on an HV EV system may be visible. It is important to give an indication to all the status of the system. This done by using the following signs which should be determined by the technician or engineer who is working on the HV EV system. Multiple signs should be used and clearly visible.

You're right, in this context "there" would become a dummy subject when the sentence is made into a subordinate clause.

The rule is that when "there" begins a clause by itself, it functions as an adverb of place. But when "there" is used with a form of the verb "to be" (is, are, was, were) after it, as in "There is a man over there", it becomes a dummy subject.

So in the example you give:

There stood my friend. - Here "there" is an adverb of place, inverting the sentence.

When there stood my friend. - Here, because it's a subordinate clause introduced by "when", "there" becomes a dummy subject. The real subject ("my friend") has been left out, but "there" is still needed for grammatical completeness.

So in short, yes - when you add that sentence into a subordinate clause, "there" stops functioning as an adverb of place and instead becomes a dummy subject, as it is used with a form of "to be" (stood).

English education at the elementary level of China’s education
With the development of our country, foreign exchanges and the national consciousness of the people are growing at same time. English has been the main subject in elementary education for many years and there are always argues about we may overvalue English. As a student who start learn English at elementary school, I think English are still important bus the role that play in our elementary education should be change.
On the one hand, as the most popular language in the world, we can't give up learning English completely. Utilitarian speaking, learning English can provide more choices for your future employment and academic development as the widely use of English in the international business and the academic area. Far more than that, if you could use English, means get information from English newspaper, books, podcast and other social media, it knowing more about other cultures, and even take you into another perspectives to viewing the world. In addition, to cope with the disrupt between two language, bilingual user need to use their brain more and that make they even smarter. Learning English from early age is help to get more punctual pronunciation and build English mind in more natural way. 
On the other hand, maybe its time to change the role of English in our elementary education. Admittedly, not every one need to use English and the fact is most student will gradually forget their English knowledge due to the lack of English use. If English is not necessary for every one, why should we ask every student to learning it to pass the entrance examination. More over, it is foreseeable that in the near future, everyone can use artificial intelligence to deal with situations that require the use of English. An ordinary student who has studied English for many years may not perform better than a Chinese monolingual using artificial intelligence.
To sum up, English is still valuable to us, but we should also re-examine the need to include English in elementary education. Maybe It is a good choice to put at the same level other foreign language like Japanese to become an elective subjects that contribute to the all-round development of students.

Response: 
"Usage of mobile phones has seen a drastic increase in the recent years. Subsequently, the harmful effects of these devices on both our health and our society are becoming more and more concerning. This brings forth the question: should governments introduce new laws in order to limit the usage of mobile devices to those who strictly need them for their work?

Firstly, although there is no clear evidence that the usage of mobile phones directly impacts the quality of life in the modern world, there have been studies suggesting that the overall effect of such devices have indeed had a negative effect on the general well being of the population. This is a fair assumption given the consumptive and compulsive nature of platforms that are easily accessible through the use of cellphones such as Tiktok and Instagram. Furthermore, many users are known to spend copious amounts of time mindlessly browsing through often useless, and at times, even dangerous and misinformative content via these applications.

Secondly, regarding the impact mobile devices have on society as a whole, there is concern that real-world explorations such as simple trip down to a bar or restaurant to meet with friends and on a grander scale cross-country and international travelling is slowly becoming replaced with virtual meetings and gatherings often taking place through commonplace mobile applications such as Whatsapp and Telegram.

In my humble opinion, mobile phones somewhat eliminate the need for real-world exploration, and the addictive nature of the applications that are specifically designed not just for them but because of them. Therefor I agree that they should be restricted in at least, a small way, for the general public. Perhaps specifying the daily hours such devices can be used would be an appropriate measure.

To conclude, although there is no clear scientific evidence of mobile phones impacting our general health, there are many instances that their indirect effects can be observed. Additionally, their effects on society are quite clear in that they reduce physical human interaction to a minimum, as this has always been their very function."

   e=0
   while (c >> e) > 0:  e=e+1

   m = mtable[ ( (c<<6) >> e ) & 0x1f ]

   q=(e<<3) + m
   return q,e,m

def decode(q):  #from coded to counts  q=8*(log2(c) +1)

  c= 2**(q/8. -1)

  return c

Aelfrun, with her coat pulled tightly around her, hurried through the crowded sidewalks, her mind preoccupied with the urban legend that had captured her attention. She couldn’t shake off the feeling that there was more to the story of Area 54 than met the eye.

As she approached the newspaper office, her mind was flooded with thoughts of the recent underground bombing in Hammerlocke, the tragedy that had rocked the region. Her bosses had constantly urged her to focus on current events, to leave behind the unsettling tales and legends that seemed to lurk in the shadows. The original inspiration for getting around via moving platforms comes from classic platformer games. I played the side-scrolling Sonic the Hedgehog games as a kid, and while some sections emphasized speed, there would also frequently be slower sections of jumping onto a moving platform and using it to reach another moving platform, and so on.

As the game’s scope grew and I had to think about what its world would look like, I found inspiration in my favorite PlayStation 2 game, Ico. That game had you move around atmospheric environments in a castle full of huge structures that made you feel small and in awe. I’ve done my best to incorporate similar elements in Eye of the Temple, and to establish a great sense of verticality.

Ico also featured extensive backtracking, looping back to earlier areas with new abilities, which made the game world feel more tangible and real. This, too, is something I’ve worked hard to incorporate in Eye of the Temple, even if the scope of this game is somewhat smaller.

I've been in something akin to a level design writer's block for a long time, being able to rework individual small areas, but unable to start the major world redesign that I've been intending for over a year.

Maybe calling it writer's block is pretentious - the fact is that I've never done this sort of work before, so I may just not have developed the necessary workflows to deal with it. Anyway, I think I might have finally cracked the nut.

I've had plenty of ideas, but fragmented and not crystallized enough to get down on paper. How do you start planning a non-linear world meant to be highly interconnected and interdependent? I can talk about what eventually worked for me.

I've long pondered what type of document could help me get ideas down on paper in a quick way. In addition to text documents (glorified to-do lists) I've been using tilemaps for sketching level designs.
I've been experimenting with using Unity Tilemaps as a digital replacement for pencil level design sketches. Some success so far, although I'm really missing rotation/flipping of selection and proper multi-selection.
These tilemaps naturally lead to obsess over details though. What recently helped me move on was allowing myself to draw free-hand inaccurate lines and gloss over the contents of rooms.It's difficult because I have ideas for the rooms that are important and which informs their shapes. write a short conclusion for this "Key findings
Ways of establishing collaborative co-design in a complex stakeholder environment.

Citizen science is not inherently collaborative. Only 4% of citizen science is co-designed, and conscious effort is required to made it so. Collaboration improves citizen science in several ways, it:
•	Allows greater access to local knowledge/data.
•	Broadens participation.
•	Increases motivation of participants.
•	Improves engagement with locally based stakeholders (Taylor et al, 2023).
•	Leads to longer lasting participation.
•	Can lead to pro-environmental behaviour change, and alterations to local land management.
•	Is more likely to lead to nature-based, locally appropriate solution selection.
There are potential drawbacks to co-design. It requires more time and effort, often on the part of both researcher and citizen scientists. It can also take decision making power away from researchers. However, the literature is overwhelmingly positive on the impact of co-design on citizen science. Effective co-design in citizen science requires collaboration at multiple stages of the project, from inception, to planning, to implementation, and ongoing usage of data gathered. Citizen science collaboration can be grouped into three broad stages: co-design, co-production of knowledge, and dissemination. The literature provides a checklist for co-designing a project:
•	Collective design of a methodology
•	Consider the needs of users and decision makers.
•	Translate user suggestions into designs (multiple, iterative cycles if necessary)
•	Design project tools (apps, surveys etc.) through a series of collaborative brainstorms
•	Create tool prototypes.
•	User testing
•	Review, further iterative designs (if necessary)
The next stage is co-production of knowledge. This is a two-way process where researchers must work to maintain scientific rigor of the project, and citizen scientists must (alongside data gathering) communicate emerging project needs to the researchers or steering committee. The dissemination stage is particularly important for the creation of communities of practice. This involves storing and sharing the information gathered in open access format, with open forums from participants to help decide how to use and interpret the data. Project specific social media apps have been successfully used to create these ongoing communities. 
How to develop and facilitate communities of practice/knowledge.
New communities of practice/knowledge can develop through citizen science projects. Existing groups can also be developed into stronger associations, or change their practices/worldviews through such projects. Intent, on the part of the researchers, is not enough to develop new communities of practice/knowledge. Such communities develop organically, but researchers can develop ideal conditions for them. 
To develop the best conditions for communities of practice to develop, the first step is co-design. This not only creates a sense of ownership, but it also allows the needs of communities to be fulfilled. Communities are more likely to form when there is a sense of partnership, as it a chance to learn something about their local area, rather than just provide data to researchers.
The next step to develop communities is knowledge management. During the data gathering stage, the utilization of multiple forms of knowledge (i.e, historical anecdotes and statistical data) helps the varied perspectives of participants feel included. Developing long-term communities can be achieved by effective storage and dissemination of knowledge, as mentioned in the previous section. Providing forums for the community to interact through also helps develop long term associations, both with researchers, and amongst themselves. These could be regular meetings/events, or social media apps dedicated to the project. Without such avenues, communities of practice tend to dissipate over time. 
Knowledge Application can improve community cohesion. This is partially because it gives further ownership and partnership of projects. Location-based communities of practice also tend to favour more nature-based, location specific solutions than researcher communities. 
Making citizen science effective and inclusive.
Exclusion tends to be most prominent in already disenfranchised groups. With those in the DE grade of the social grade system (Semi-skilled & unskilled manual occupations, Unemployed and lowest grade occupations) being least likely to participate. Though younger people are generally less likely to participate, their numbers have shown an upward trend in recent years.
As disenfranchised groups are more likely to have direct experience of degraded environments, their exclusion from citizen science can affect data quality. Below is a chart showing the effects of background on participation in citizen science projects:


Variable	Most likely cohort to participate (% of sampled group)	Least likely cohort to participate (% of sampled group)	
Gender	Men (8.3%)	Women (6.8%)	
Age	55-64 (9.3%)	25–34 (4.1%)

Social Grade	Grade B (16.7%)	Grade DE (3.3%)	
Area (Urban/Rural)	Urban (80.9%)	Rural (8.7%)	

There are multiple strategies for improving inclusion in citizen science, such as:
•	Inclusion focused recruitment strategies
•	Instituting flexible project structure
•	Accommodation those with different experience backgrounds
•	Providing forms of compensation for participants
•	Co-designing the project.

user_prompt:
我会提供给你内容：Previous work on generative language models qualitatively tested their ability to generate synthetic “news articles” by
conditional sampling from the model given a human-written prompt consisting of a plausible first sentence for a news
story [RWC+19]. Relative to [RWC+19], the dataset used to train GPT-3 is much less weighted towards news articles,
so trying to generate news articles via raw unconditional samples is less effective – for example GPT-3 often interprets
the proposed first sentence of a “news article” as a tweet and then posts synthetic responses or follow-up tweets. To
solve this problem we employed GPT-3’s few-shot learning abilities by providing three previous news articles in the
model’s context to condition it. With the title and subtitle of a proposed next article, the model is able to reliably
generate short articles in the “news” genre.
To gauge the quality of news article generation from GPT-3 (which we believe is likely to be correlated with conditional
sample generation quality in general), we decided to measure human ability to distinguish GPT-3-generated articles
from real ones. Similar work has been carried out by Kreps et al. [KMB20] and Zellers et al. [ZHR+19]. Generative
language models are trained to match the distribution of content generated by humans, so the (in)ability of humans to
distinguish the two is a potentially important measure of quality.3
In order to see how well humans can detect model generated text, we arbitrarily selected 25 article titles and subtitles
from the website newser.com (mean length: 215 words). We then generated completions of these titles and subtitles
from four language models ranging in size from 125M to 175B (GPT-3) parameters (mean length: 200 words). For each
model, we presented around 80 US-based participants with a quiz consisting of these real titles and subtitles followed
by either the human written article or the article generated by the model4
. Participants were asked to select whether the
article was “very likely written by a human”, “more likely written by a human”, “I don’t know”, “more likely written by
a machine”, or “very likely written by a machine”.
The articles we selected were not in the models’ training data and the model outputs were formatted and selected
programmatically to prevent human cherry-picking. All models used the same context to condition outputs on and were
pre-trained with the same context size and the same article titles and subtitles were used as prompts for each model.
However, we also ran an experiment to control for participant effort and attention that followed the same format but
involved intentionally bad model generated articles. This was done by generating articles from a “control model”: a
160M parameter model with no context and increased output randomness.

  SELECT 
    id, ARRAY[id]
  FROM topics 
  WHERE parent = 0
  UNION 
  SELECT 
    t.id, path || t.id
  FROM 
    topics t
    INNER JOIN topic_parent rt ON rt.id = t.parent
),
cte2 as (
  select *, unnest(path) AS linked_id
  from topic_parent
)

inner join tasks_topics t on c.id = t.topics_id
inner join tasks t2 on t2.id = t.task_id
inner join topics t3 on t3.id = c.linked_id
group by task_id, linked_id
order by task_id asc, linked_id desc Как работает этот рекурсивный запрос?

The cold start problem of new users is a common problem in all recommendation systems due to the lack of information about new users in the system [10]. The lack of available user data in the situation where new users/ users join the system limits the effectiveness of the news recommender system to suggest relevant news to this kind of user. Due to this insufficient user data, there is an occurrence of a new user cold-start problem. This user data is divided into two, explicit data which is collected by the reader’s direct activity (i.e., when users give feedback directly to the news articles while she/ he is reading) and implicit data which the system collects by following the reader’s activities (i.e., using the reader’s link navigation behaviour including the time spent to read articles) in the system. These user data are not sufficient in order to suggest and recommend relevant news articles to the readers in the scenario where a new user joins the system [1], [3], [4]. Therefore, we proposed to use demographic data of the user for the new user to start the system.

For example, some readers need only a specific field of news that is more related to their profession. Whereas, others users want to read a more general field (i.e., sports or entertainment). This news recommendation system is used to help the users on their interest of news and to provide updated news for the users based on their interests.

As our proposed system is to fix the problem of new user interest of news, the system will fix it and recommend news for the user according to user groups and their patterns of interest. In addition, it recommends popular news by filtering the articles most read by many users and obtaining the highest rate value. And the user should recommend only the categories that s/he is more interested in. For example, if he/she is interested in entertainment news, he/she should have to get from this category and the same for other news categories. The system returns the news to all new users and existing users, which is category-based (i.e., the news to be recommended/predicted will be the category of news that users want to read).

The second one is how to figure out this impact on the new recommender scheme towards performance metrics such as Precision, Recall, and F1-Score. The last one is, how to model a new recommender system for a new user.

WITH RECURSIVE topic_parent(id, path) AS 
    (SELECT id,
         ARRAY[id]
    FROM topics
    WHERE parent = 0
    UNION
    SELECT t.id,
         path || t.id
    FROM topics t
    INNER JOIN topic_parent rt
        ON rt.id = t.parent ), limited_tasks AS 
    (SELECT * FROM public.tasks
    ORDER BY id ASC 
     LIMIT 100 )
SELECT limited_tasks.id,
         limited_tasks.task,
         limited_tasks.answer,
         array_agg(DISTINCT topics.name) AS topic_name
FROM limited_tasks
INNER JOIN tasks_topics
    ON limited_tasks.id = tasks_topics.task_id
INNER JOIN 
    (SELECT *,
         unnest(path) AS linked_id
    FROM topic_parent) cte2
    ON cte2.id = tasks_topics.topics_id
INNER JOIN topics
    ON topics.id = cte2.linked_id
GROUP BY  limited_tasks.id, limited_tasks.task, limited_tasks.answer
ORDER BY  limited_tasks.id ASC

(Just the sheer cold of the glacier biome made me ever regret coming here in the first place.)

[player]: “BRRRRRRRR! This place is cold.”

(Just then, I noticed a massive palace in the distance. It didn’t look that menacing from a distance.)

[player]: “Hopefully it’s not as cold as out here.”

(I walked inside, and saw that this place was made out of a strange-looking block I’ve never seen before - called the “Aurora Block”. And then, I felt something ram into my side.)

Female Unstable Ice Core: (fast-speaking and erratic) “Oh boy, a visitor! You have no idea how bored I was!”

[player]: “Uh…”

(I noticed that one of the girl’s eyes was purple, but the other was lavender.)

[player]: “Do you…have a name?”

Female Unstable Ice Core: “Eh…not really. Our creator - the Snow Queen - doesn't even name us, even after we’re created.”

(Just then, we could hear the Snow Queen screaming in pain from the top of the Aurora Palace.)

[player]: “Is she alright? What’s happening up there?”

Female Unstable Ice Core: “I-I-I don’t know! Do you think we should check on her?”

[player]: “Yes, we should definitely go and check on her. It sounds like she’s in a lot of pain.”

(I followed the unstable ice core as she led me through the grand corridors of the Aurora Palace. The walls were adorned with intricate ice sculptures and shimmering crystals, giving off an ethereal glow. It was both captivating and otherworldly.)

(As we ascended the palace, the screams of the Snow Queen grew louder and more agonized. My heart raced, and I couldn’t help but worry for her well-being. The unstable ice core, with her mismatched eyes, seemed equally concerned.)

(Eventually, we reached a chamber at the highest point of the palace. The room was filled with swirling snowflakes and intense cold. In the center, lying on the floor, was the Snow Queen. She was clutching her swollen belly, and writhing in pain.)

[player]: “Snow Queen, are you alright? What’s happening?”

(The Snow Queen continued to scream in pain. Just from how much her stomach was swollen, something was wrong with her.)

Female Unstable Ice Core: “Is it the frostbite?! Is everything okay?!”

(The Snow Queen shook her head. But the reason why she was feeling so much pain was something we weren’t expecting.)

WITH RECURSIVE topic_parent(id, path) AS 
    (SELECT id,
         ARRAY[id]
    FROM topics
    WHERE parent = 0
    UNION
    SELECT t.id,
         path || t.id
    FROM topics t
    INNER JOIN topic_parent rt
        ON rt.id = t.parent ), limited_tasks AS 
    (SELECT * FROM public.tasks
    ORDER BY id ASC 
     LIMIT 100 )
SELECT limited_tasks.id,
         limited_tasks.task,
         limited_tasks.answer,
         array_agg(DISTINCT topics.name) AS topic_name
FROM limited_tasks
INNER JOIN tasks_topics
    ON limited_tasks.id = tasks_topics.task_id
INNER JOIN 
    (SELECT *,
         unnest(path) AS linked_id
    FROM topic_parent) cte2
    ON cte2.id = tasks_topics.topics_id
INNER JOIN topics
    ON topics.id = cte2.linked_id
GROUP BY  limited_tasks.id, limited_tasks.task, limited_tasks.answer
ORDER BY  limited_tasks.id ASC

class Tasks(db.Model):
    __tablename__ = 'tasks'
    __searchable__ = ['task','id']  # these fields will be indexed by whoosh

    id = db.Column(db.Integer, primary_key=True, autoincrement=True)
    url = db.Column(db.String(120), comment="ЧПУ задачи в адресе (транслитом)")
    task = db.Column(db.Text, comment='Условие задачи')
    answer = db.Column(db.Text, comment='Ответ')
    status = db.Column(db.Boolean, default=0, comment='Статус: опубликована/неактивна (по умолчанию нет)')
    created_t = db.Column(db.DateTime, comment='Дата и время создания')
    level = db.Column(db.SmallInteger, default=1, comment='Уровень сложности: 1,2 ... (по умолчанию 1 уровень)')

    # связи
    topics = db.relationship('Topics',
                            secondary=tasks_topics,
                            back_populates="tasks")


class Topics(db.Model):
    __tablename__ = 'topics'
    __searchable__ = ['name']

    id = db.Column(db.Integer, primary_key=True, autoincrement=True)
    name = db.Column(db.String(140), comment="Уникальное название темы(подтемы)")
    parent = db.Column(db.Integer, default=0, comment="ID родительской темы(если есть)")

    # связи
    tasks = db.relationship('Tasks',
                            secondary=tasks_topics,
                            back_populates="topics")

         ARRAY[id]
    FROM topics

    UNION

    FROM topics t
    INNER JOIN topic_parent rt
        ON rt.id = t.parent ), limited_tasks AS 
    (SELECT * FROM public.tasks

         limited_tasks.task,
         limited_tasks.answer,
         array_agg(DISTINCT topics.name) AS topic_name

INNER JOIN tasks_topics
    ON limited_tasks.id = tasks_topics.task_id

         unnest(path) AS linked_id
    FROM topic_parent) cte2
    ON cte2.id = tasks_topics.topics_id

    ON topics.id = cte2.linked_id
GROUP BY  limited_tasks.id, limited_tasks.task, limited_tasks.answer
ORDER BY  limited_tasks.id ASC

WITH RECURSIVE topic_parent(id, path) AS 
    (SELECT id,
         ARRAY[id]
    FROM topics
    WHERE parent = 0
    UNION
    SELECT t.id,
         path || t.id
    FROM topics t
    INNER JOIN topic_parent rt
        ON rt.id = t.parent ), limited_tasks AS 
    (SELECT * FROM public.tasks
    ORDER BY id ASC 
     LIMIT 100 )
SELECT limited_tasks.id,
         limited_tasks.task,
         limited_tasks.answer,
         array_agg(DISTINCT topics.name) AS topic_name
FROM limited_tasks
INNER JOIN tasks_topics
    ON limited_tasks.id = tasks_topics.task_id
INNER JOIN 
    (SELECT *,
         unnest(path) AS linked_id
    FROM topic_parent) cte2
    ON cte2.id = tasks_topics.topics_id
INNER JOIN topics
    ON topics.id = cte2.linked_id
GROUP BY  limited_tasks.id, limited_tasks.task, limited_tasks.answer
ORDER BY  limited_tasks.id ASC

Есть запрос в potresql

WITH RECURSIVE topic_parent(id, path) AS 
    (SELECT id,
         ARRAY[id]
    FROM topics
    WHERE parent = 0
    UNION
    SELECT t.id,
         path || t.id
    FROM topics t
    INNER JOIN topic_parent rt
        ON rt.id = t.parent ), limited_tasks AS 
    (SELECT * FROM public.tasks
    ORDER BY id ASC 
     LIMIT 100 )
SELECT limited_tasks.id,
         limited_tasks.task,
         limited_tasks.answer,
         array_agg(DISTINCT topics.name) AS topic_name
FROM limited_tasks
INNER JOIN tasks_topics
    ON limited_tasks.id = tasks_topics.task_id
INNER JOIN 
    (SELECT *,
         unnest(path) AS linked_id
    FROM topic_parent) cte2
    ON cte2.id = tasks_topics.topics_id
INNER JOIN topics
    ON topics.id = cte2.linked_id
GROUP BY  limited_tasks.id, limited_tasks.task, limited_tasks.answer
ORDER BY  limited_tasks.id ASC

user_prompt:
ваш термин о tree-based, совпадает с этим: This decompiler works by processing the Binary Space Partitioning tree for hull 0 (point hull) for each brush model.

The world itself is model 0 and contains all brushes not tied to a brush entity. Each brush entity adds one brush model to the map.

The process used to generate brushes works by first calculating the bounding box for the model, then adding 8 units extra to it to account for walls on the outermost brush faces in the map.

A brush of that size is then created, and is split in 2 repeatedly by walking the BSP tree.

The resulting set of brushes is an approximate representation of the original map, but is not perfectly accurate.

The texturing phase tries to find the faces that the generated brush faces are the closest match to.

If brush optimization is set to best texture match the brush is split if needed to more closely match the original brush face.

If brush merging is enabled brushes that are found to have the same contents (e.g. solid, water, etc) and texture properties and that form a convex brush are merged together.

Finally, each brush is converted to its map source file representation.

Brushes that have no textures on any faces are skipped. This includes brushes that originated as CLIP or NULL textured brushes. This can leave some brush entities without any brushes.
